strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem statement: the locality of windowed self-attention in PDE foundation models (scOT/POSEIDON) and the resulting rollout drift are convincingly argued.

The dual-branch design (controlled low-frequency spectral mixing + image branch with bandwise radial gating and non-expensive additive fusion) is clearly described, with code-aligned pseudocode and implementation details in the appendix.

Experiments use a matched-budget, matched-protocol comparison against scOT and FNO on the POSEIDON benchmark suite plus two long-horizon ApeBench Kolmogorov variants, with additional rollout curves (mean error, growth slope) beyond final-time metrics.

Ablations isolate each component (LFM, radial gating, frequency-weighted loss) on two tasks, and bandwise nRMSE spectral analysis supports the mechanistic claims about mid/high-frequency error suppression.

Efficiency results (17M vs 20M parameters, 158 vs 118 steps/s) support the efficiency claims, and the appendix provides Lipschitz/energy-bounds and a discrete Grönwall-style argument giving the paper some theoretical grounding.
Honest limitations section acknowledging hand-tuned spectral cutoffs, FFT memory cost, and restriction to 2D.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: the core recipe (U-Net image branch + FFT-based spectral branch with low-frequency channel mixing + frequency-weighted auxiliary loss) is a recombination of well-known components from FNO, U-NO, AFNO/Global Filter Networks, and focal frequency loss; the bandwise radial gating is an incremental refinement rather than a fundamentally new mechanism.

Narrow empirical scope: only Navier–Stokes-family benchmarks are evaluated; despite framing around 'PDE foundation models,' no transfer, cross-equation, or cross-resolution experiments are shown, and the authors themselves admit 2D-only, regular-domain settings.

Weak baseline set: only scOT and FNO are compared, and FNO performs implausibly poorly (e.g., 9.46 on NS-Tracer-PwC), raising tuning concerns; missing modern strong baselines such as U-NO, AFNO, CNO, PDE-Refiner, and poseidon ablations.

No statistical rigor: results are single-run test means with no seeds, standard deviations, or significance tests; several margins (e.g., FNS-KF 4.315 vs 4.647, a 7.2% gap) are small enough that run-to-run variance could matter.

Theoretical contributions are thin: Lemma A.3 is a one-line convexity argument, and Proposition A.2's 'tighter cumulative bound' essentially assumes the comparison condition it needs, so the stability claims are weaker than the abstract implies; no experimental validation of the Grönwall-type bound is provided.

Presentation issues: the code URL in the abstract is missing/truncated; Appendix E ('Pseudocode') is empty; Figure 5's channel-0 visualization is an uninformative solid-color panel; throughput is reported 'under a different resolution and precision configuration' with both numbers repeated inconsistently, which is sloppy.

Hyperparameters of the frequency-weighted loss (λ, α) and the low-frequency mask cutoffs are hand-tuned with no sensitivity analysis; the method's dependence on these choices is unclear and limits reproducibility and generality.

Evaluation inconsistencies: Table 2 is labeled an 'additional subset' yet duplicates the main POSEIDON results; the text cites both 19.1% and 19.1%/53.6% improvements in ways that require careful reconciliation, and the foundation-model positioning is not backed by any foundation-style evaluation.

strengths: The paper is clearly written and well organized, with a coherent motivation: windowed self-attention (scOT/POSEIDON) builds global coupling only gradually across depth, which can drive rollout drift.

The proposed unit is modular and reasonably simple: controlled low-frequency spectral mixing, bandwise convex (radial-gated) fusion, and a frequency-weighted loss, with a non-expansive design that avoids channel-width inflation.

The evaluation follows the POSEIDON protocol with matched training budgets, reports parameter counts and throughput, includes ablations of all three components (Table 4), bandwise error analysis over time (Fig. 4), and error-vs-time rollout curves (Figs. 2-3).
The code-aligned pseudocode (Algorithm 1) and appendix implementation details improve reproducibility relative to typical architecture papers.
Limitations are candidly acknowledged (hand-tuned frequency cutoff, memory cost of FFTs in every block, 2D-only scope).
weaknesses: Limited novelty. The components are straightforward combinations of well-established ideas: FNO/AFNO-style spectral channel mixing, U-Net branch fusion (U-FNO, U-NO, GFNet), gating reminiscent of SE/squeeze-excitation, and frequency-weighted losses essentially equivalent to focal frequency loss (Jiang et al., 2021). The 'controlled low-frequency mixing' and convex bandwise gating are incremental over this prior art, and the paper does not clearly delineate what is new beyond an engineering assembly of known pieces.

Baseline coverage is thin. Only scOT and (a seemingly weak) FNO are compared, despite the paper's positioning against 'PDE foundation models'. No comparison to PDE-Refiner (explicitly cited for drift), U-NO, CNO, AFNO, or POSEIDON's full model. The very poor FNO numbers suggest possible suboptimal tuning of baselines.

Evaluation rigor is insufficient for the claims: results are single-run means with no variance, seeds, or significance testing; ablations are limited to two tasks; gains on the hardest long-horizon tasks are marginal (KF-Long turbulent 110.87 vs 114.14, smoother 57.17 vs 62.99) with relative errors >100, i.e., effectively divergent rollouts where differences are hard to interpret.

The theoretical contributions are decorative rather than substantive. Lemma A.1 and Proposition A.2 are trivial norm inequalities, and the 'Sobolev-weighted one-step defect bound' (Thm B.1) is a sketch with assumptions not connected to actual training; none of the theory is empirically validated or used to make design decisions.

Internal inconsistencies in reporting undermine confidence: the text itself notes that the throughput numbers (158 vs 118 steps/s) come from 'a different resolution and precision configuration' than Table 3, and Table 1/Table 2 subsets with slightly differing values are confusingly presented rather than reconciled.

Key hyperparameters (lambda, alpha of the frequency-weighted loss, number of radial bands, cutoff initialization) are described only as 'moderate values suffice', which is too vague for reproducibility and raises concerns about tuning effort spent on the proposed method versus baselines.

The qualitative visualization (Fig. 5) is essentially unusable (channel 0 is a flat dark field), and Figure 4 has unclear legends/labels, so the spectral-analysis claims are hard to verify from the presented evidence.

Scope is narrow: only 2D periodic Navier-Stokes variants; no irregular geometries, boundary conditions, or 3D cases, which limits the significance of the 'modular unit for PDE foundation models' claim.

strengths: Clear motivation and positioning: the paper identifies a concrete weakness of windowed-attention PDE backbones (slow, depth-dependent global coupling) and proposes an explicit spectral path as a remedy, which is a sensible and well-articulated design hypothesis.

The bandwise fusion with radial gating (Eq. 4.2) with a convexity-based non-expansiveness argument (Eq. 4.3) is a clean, simple mechanism, and the ablation (Table 4) plus bandwise nRMSE spectral analysis (Fig. 4) provides component-level evidence that each part contributes.

Evaluation follows the POSEIDON protocol with matched data budget and hardware, reports parameter count and throughput, and adds two long-horizon (T=100) Kolmogorov variants, which addresses rollout drift rather than only one-step error.

Appendix contains some theoretical content (per-block Lipschitz bounds, discrete Grönwall implication, Sobolev-weighted defect bound) and a code-aligned pseudocode block, which aids reproducibility of the method description.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: dual-branch spectral + spatial operator designs are well explored (FNO, U-FNO, AFNO, GFNO, Ghost-style modulators), and the frequency-weighted auxiliary loss is essentially the known focal frequency loss. The contribution reduces to a specific gated low-band mixing + residual fusion recipe; no comparison or discussion against these closely related hybrids is provided in the experiments.

Narrow baseline set: only scOT and FNO are compared. Missing strong modern baselines (U-NO, CNO, AFNO, PDE-Refiner, the full POSEIDON model, and a plain U-Net/ConvNeXt control without the spectral branch) makes it hard to judge whether gains come from the proposed fusion or simply from adding Fourier mixing to a conv U-Net.

Weaker and inconsistent headline claims: the abstract claims 7%-54% error reduction, but the tables show ~3% on KF-Long (turbulent) and ~9% on the smoother variant, and errors around 110 relative L1 at T=100 indicate both models essentially diverge, so the 'long-horizon robustness' claim is overstated. Table 1 vs. Table 2 values (2.350 vs. 2.350 OK, but text quotes NS-PwC as 'reported in prior results' with different provenance) and the truncated abstract/code link ('available at') plus throughput reported twice under different settings (158 vs. 118 vs. Table 3) suggest a rushed manuscript.

No variance reporting: all results are single-run test means with no seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests, despite differences of a few percent on some tasks; the hand-tuned initial frequency cutoff (acknowledged in limitations) further weakens generality claims.

Theory-practice mismatch: Proposition A.2 and the Lipschitz comparison to Swin blocks assume K_lin <= 1 (spectral-ball projection of W), yet Sec. 4.2 states W is deliberately left unconstrained; the stability story therefore does not strictly apply to the model actually trained, and the Grönwall/defect bounds are not empirically validated.

2D-only, periodic-domain evaluation on four (plus two) benchmarks; no transfer, resolution generalization, or foundation-model-style experiments despite framing the unit as a drop-in for PDE foundation models.

Qualitative visualization (Fig. 5) is largely uninformative (channel 0 panels are uniformly dark, single example), and Figure 2/3 axis labeling and text-to-figure consistency (e.g., slope numbers) are hard to verify.

strengths: Well-executed, transparent empirical study: matched training budgets, splits, optimizer, and hardware across all baselines, following the established POSEIDON protocol, which makes the head-to-head comparison with scOT credible.

Consistent empirical gains across seven benchmark tasks spanning different PDE types (Navier-Stokes, elliptic, parabolic, hyperbolic), plus long-horizon (T=100) closed-loop rollouts with error-growth and instantaneous-error analyses that directly probe the claimed drift-reduction mechanism.

Thorough ablations (LFM, radial gating, frequency-weighted loss, image-branch components) with bandwise spectral error analysis that connects each component to its intended frequency-domain effect, plus additional width-scaling, learning-rate-sensitivity, sample-efficiency, and cross-resolution experiments in the appendix.
Clear efficiency story: fewer parameters (~15%), lower peak training memory, faster training, and higher inference throughput than scOT at matched and half width.
Honest limitations section (hand-tuned low-frequency cutoff, FFT cost on large grids, 2D-only evaluation) and reasonable motivation grounded in the locality of windowed attention.
Reproducibility appears strong: detailed hyperparameters, dataset shapes and splits, pseudocode, and stated code release.
weaknesses: Limited architectural novelty: combining a Fourier/spectral branch with a convolutional branch is well explored (U-FNO, GFNet, AFNO, CNO, FNO variants). The learnable low-frequency mask, radial bandwise gating, and frequency-weighted loss are refinements of existing ideas rather than a fundamentally new mechanism, and the paper does not compare against any of these closely related spectral–spatial hybrids.

The theoretical analysis in Appendix A is shallow and largely restates trivial facts: the 'energy non-expansive' bound is one-line convexity, the Lipschitz bound is standard composition, and Proposition A.2 is conditional on an assumption that essentially assumes the conclusion; the Gronwall 'implication' does not establish anything about actual rollout drift of trained models.
The claimed causal link between weakened global spectral coupling and rollout drift is asserted via citation but never demonstrated experimentally beyond indirect error curves.

Potential fairness concern: DRIFT-Net uses a frequency-weighted auxiliary loss (Eq. 4.4) that is not granted to baselines under the 'identical training settings' claim, so part of the reported gain may come from the loss rather than the architecture; no baseline is trained with FWL.

No error bars, confidence intervals, or multi-seed variance for any experiment, despite gains on some tasks being small (e.g., FNS-KF 4.32 vs 4.38; NS-SL 3.40 vs 3.48); statistical significance of these differences is unverifiable.

Baselines are restricted to scOT-T (tiny, ~20M), FNO, U-NO, and two U-Net variants; stronger modern operator transformers (DPOT, Transolver, GNOT, OFormer) and pretrained-foundation-model settings are absent, limiting the evidence that DRIFT-Net is competitive as a backbone for future PDE foundation models.
Scope is narrow: only 2D problems on a fixed 128×128 grid; the cross-resolution test (Table 9) is essentially in-distribution interpolation, so claims of mesh-agnostic behavior are weakly supported.

Presentation issues: the code URL in the abstract is empty; Appendix G explicitly refers to 'reviewer questions in the rebuttal,' which is inappropriate framing for a submission; some claims (e.g., '7%–54% error reduction') span results of very different magnitude and should be broken down per task.

strengths: Evaluation follows the established POSEIDON protocol with matched data budgets, splits, optimizer, and training schedules across all baselines, which makes the comparison relatively fair and reproducible.

Broad empirical coverage: seven downstream PDE tasks (Navier–Stokes variants, Allen–Cahn, Wave–Gauss, Poisson–Gauss) plus two long-horizon ApeBench Kolmogorov rollouts (T=100), with efficiency measurements (parameters, memory, throughput) and width-scaling (Table 3/5).

Component-wise ablations (LFM, radial gating, frequency-weighted loss, image-branch operators) plus bandwise spectral error analysis (Figure 4) support the design claims about mid/high-frequency error suppression.

The paper is honest about limitations (hand-tuned low-frequency cutoff, 2D-only, FFT memory traffic on large grids), and appendix materials (pseudocode, hyperparameters, datasets) are detailed enough to support reproducibility.
weaknesses: Limited novelty. The core components are well-established: FFT-domain low-frequency channel mixing is essentially FNO/GFNet-style global filtering (Rao et al., 2021 is cited), radial bandwise gating is a smooth variant of spectral masking, and the frequency-weighted loss closely mirrors focal frequency loss (Jiang et al., 2021). The dual spectral–spatial U-Net combination (cf. U-FNO, CNO, U-NO) is incremental, and the paper does not clearly articulate what is fundamentally new beyond recombining known pieces.

The theoretical contribution is largely trivial or vacuous. Lemma A.3 is a one-line convexity argument; Proposition A.2 is a conditional statement ('if the constants are smaller, the product is smaller') that provides no evidence the constants are actually smaller in practice; Theorem B.1 is only a proof sketch and is never connected to observed rollout behavior. No experiments verify the claimed Lipschitz/stability benefits (e.g., gradient norms, rollout variance).

Empirical gains are inconsistent and often marginal. On NS-SL (3.48→3.40), FNS-KF (4.38→4.32), and Poisson–Gauss (0.87→0.86) improvements are within what could plausibly be run-to-run noise, yet no error bars, standard deviations, or multiple-seed results are reported anywhere. The 7%–54% headline is driven mainly by one task (NS-PwC).

Long-horizon results are weak in absolute terms: final relative L1 errors of 110.87 vs. 114.14 (turbulent) and 57.17 vs. 62.99 (smoother) mean both models essentially diverge; the claimed robustness advantage is modest against this backdrop and only compared against scOT.

Baseline coverage has gaps: the Refiner U-Net baseline is missing on Poisson–Gauss; stronger recent spectral–attention hybrids and frequency-domain transformers (e.g., AFNO/GFNet-style operator baselines, GAP transformer) are not compared; only two models (scOT, DRIFT-Net) are evaluated in the long-horizon section.

The low-frequency cutoff is admitted to be hand-tuned per task, which weakens the 'identical training settings' fairness claim and raises a mild risk of per-task tuning; the learning-rate/schedule sensitivity study (Appendix G.2) is confined to a single task (FNS-KF).

Positioning overstates significance: the paper frames DRIFT-Net as a modular backbone for PDE foundation models, but all experiments are from-scratch single-task training on 128×128 2D grids; no pretraining, multi-task, or transfer results substantiate the foundation-model claim.

Presentation issues: the abstract ends with an incomplete sentence ('The code is available at' with no URL); Figure 5's Channel 0 panel is uninformative (uniformly dark); Figure 4 subpanels are illegible at the printed scale; some efficiency claims (e.g., 'matches asymptotic complexity of window attention') are asserted without rigorous accounting.

strengths: The paper is well-motivated: the locality of windowed self-attention in multi-scale PDE foundation backbones (scOT/POSEIDON) and its connection to rollout drift is a reasonable and timely observation, and the dual-branch spectral/spatial design directly targets it.

Evaluation is conducted under a carefully matched protocol: identical splits, data budgets, epoch budgets, optimizer, and hardware across all baselines, which strengthens the credibility of the accuracy and efficiency comparisons.

The benchmark coverage is broad and appropriate: four POSEIDON Navier-Stokes tasks plus elliptic (Poisson-Gauss), parabolic (Allen-Cahn), and hyperbolic (Wave-Gauss) PDEs, and dedicated long-horizon (T=100) closed-loop experiments with error-growth slope analysis, which goes beyond final-time metrics.

The ablation study is thorough, covering each architectural component (LFM, radial gating, FWL, and image-branch operators), and the bandwise nRMSE spectral analysis (Fig. 4) provides mechanism-level insight that connects ablations to the frequency-domain design rationale.

Efficiency results are convincing and non-trivial: fewer parameters (17M vs 20M), lower training memory, lower per-epoch time, and higher throughput than scOT, with width-scaling and learning-rate sensitivity studies in the appendix supporting robustness of the comparison.

Reproducibility is above average: detailed dataset descriptions, model configurations for every baseline, training hyperparameters, pseudocode aligned to the implementation, and a code release promise.
weaknesses: Novelty is incremental. The core idea—combining a Fourier/spectral branch for low-frequency global mixing with a convolutional branch for local detail, fused additively—is a natural combination of well-known ingredients (FNO/U-FNO spectral paths, ConvNeXt U-Nets, frequency-gated fusion as in GFNet/Global Filter Networks, which the authors themselves cite). The paper does not clearly articulate what is fundamentally new relative to this prior spectral-spatial hybrid literature, and it does not compare against those hybrids.

Baseline selection is somewhat narrow: the only strong attention-based baseline is scOT. Missing comparisons to other recent competitive operators (e.g., AFNO, CNO, or frequency-domain transformer variants) make it hard to judge whether DRIFT-Net is genuinely the best spectral-spatial design or simply a better-tuned variant of a U-Net backbone.

The theoretical analysis (Appendix A) is largely superficial: Lemma A.3 is a one-line convexity argument, and the Lipschitz/Gronwall bounds rely on conditional inequalities ('if K_DRIFT < K_SWIN') that do not establish when the condition holds in practice. The 'theoretical analyses' claimed in the abstract overstate the substance.

Improvements on the hardest, most relevant setting—long-horizon turbulent rollout—are modest (110.87 vs 114.14, about 3%), and the paper's central claim that locality-induced spectral coupling causes rollout drift is supported mainly by correlational evidence rather than a controlled demonstration.

The low-frequency cutoff mask is hand-tuned and task-specific, as acknowledged in the limitations; no sensitivity study of the mask cutoff is provided, leaving open how much of the gain depends on this hyperparameter.

Presentation issues: Figure 4 panels are too small to read; the abstract's code link is incomplete ('The code is available at'); Appendix G explicitly references 'reviewer questions in the rebuttal,' which reads as an artifact rather than self-contained content.

All experiments are 2D on a fixed 128x128 grid; cross-resolution results (Table 9) only show nearly identical errors at similar resolutions, which is a weak test of the resolution-generalization claims typical for neural operators.
